newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Compaq says profits rise by two-thirds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Compaq says profits rise by two-thirds.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. said Wednesday its profits jumped by two-thirds to $387 million in the first quarter, although revenue was slightly less than some expectations.
Compaq, the world's largest supplier of personal computers, said its net income for the first quarter rose to $387 million, or $1.36 a share, from $234 million, or 85 cents a share, a year earlier.
The earnings per share were slightly better than the $1.31 that Wall Street had expected, according to First Call, which tracks financial analysts' estimates.
Houston-based Compaq said its worldwide sales grew 14.3 percent to $4.8 billion from $4.2 billion in the first quarter of 1996, although some analysts said revenues came in below expectations.
"It was a resoundingly neutral quarter,'" said Louis Mazzucchelli, a Gerard Klauer Mattison analyst.
Compaq Chief Financial Officer Earl Mason said in an interview that revenues were hurt by currency fluctuations, as the stronger dollar overseas translated into lower revenues in the United States.
"It probably affected revenues by $200 million but it didn't affect earnings at all," Mason said.
Compaq also had a tough comparison with the first quarter of 1996, when its revenues soared 42 percent.
"My estimate was $4.9 billion in revenues," said Daniel Ries, a Nomura Research analyst. "You can make the case that it was somewhat light."
Compaq said its first-quarter gross profit margins rose to 24.5 percent from 24.4 percent in the 1996 fourth quarter, and its cash pile climbed to $4.7 billion.
Profits were boosted by sales of higher profit margin products, such as server computers, its new workstations, and storage products, analysts said.

"Sales of enterprise-class systems were a clear bright spot in the results," Ries said, adding that sales of these systems, which include server and workstation computers and data communications equipment, grew 58 percent year-over-year and accounted for 29 percent of total revenue.
"It's a good solid quarter," he said. "The asset management is phenomenal."
The company said its focus on asset management reduced its inventory by $666 million from the 1996 first quarter.

"We're very pleased with the consistency of our financial progress, especially with the improvements in earnings and the growth of gross margins to 24.5 percent," Compaq Chief Executive Officer Eckhard Pfeiffer said in a statement. "We expect strong growth throughout 1997."
Compaq's growing cash pile has fueled speculation recently on Wall Street it was considering a big acquisition.
Mason said Compaq will use its cash to expand the company but declined to talk about any specific plans. "We continue to study lots of different things," he said.

Mason declined to comment on Compaq's recent talks to buy Micron Electronics Inc., which were confirmed on Friday in a statement by both Micron Electronics and Micron Technology Inc. Micron Technology still owns 64 percent of Micron Electronics, a direct seller of PCs.
The companies said they were "not currently engaged in active discussions" with Compaq.
Compaq's Mason also refused to comment about recent rumors that the company was in talks to buy Gateway 2000 Inc.
"We want to grow our data communications and networking business," Mason said. Last week, Compaq announced a deal to buy Microcom Inc. for about $280 million.
Some analysts said they were concerned about Compaq's outlook for the second quarter.

"We heard the words 'seasonal' and 'normal' come out of Eckhard's mouth (in a conference call)," said Mark Specker, a SoundView Financial analyst. "Second-quarter demand sounds good but it was sounding seasonal."
Mason said he was comfortable with analysts' estimates of profits equal to $1.37 a share for the second quarter and that revenues would be "fine" but he also cautioned about further currency impact.
Compaq's stock fell $1.25 to $73.375 on the New York Stock Exchange, after earlier rising as high as $76.875.
